idiom_name: rule table of function pointers or lambdas + binding-power loop
implementation_notes: The classic C++ form is a table of handlers - plain function pointers or capturing lambdas stored in std::function - keyed by token kind, plus a parseExpr(minBp) loop, with binding powers as constexpr ints and token payloads in a std::variant or a small struct. No C++ library provides the Pratt loop, so the structure is hand-written; std::function is convenient but allocates for larger captures and adds an indirect call, so performance-sensitive parsers keep function pointers and pass context explicitly, or use statically typed parselet objects. Choose this realization for compilers and tools that need control over error positions, allocations and AST shape; reach for a parser generator (ANTLR, Boost.Spirit, lemon/re2c) when the grammar is broader than its expression layer.
pitfalls: Storing capturing lambdas in std::function puts a heap allocation and an indirect call on the per-token path; prefer function pointers with an explicit context, or reserve/reuse the wrappers.
A table sized to the token enum that omits initializers value-initializes the row to null function pointers - calling nud/led on such a row is undefined behaviour rather than a parse error.
Handlers that hold std::string_view tokens referencing a buffer that is later moved or freed leave dangling views; keep the source buffer alive for the whole parse or copy the lexemes.
